source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (National Final)
source.paper: 2015-16 National Final, Shuttle Round, question A1

prompt: $p$ and $q$ are two different primes greater than $25$. Find the least possible value of $p+q$.

solutions.title: Smallest primes
solutions.body:
The primes above $25$ are $29,31,37,\dots$. The two smallest sum to $29+31=60$. (In the shuttle round this was passed on to A2.)

**Answer: $60$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (National Final)
source.paper: 2015-16 National Final, Shuttle Round, question A2

prompt: Let $T=60$. The digit sum of $78$ is $15$ because $7+8=15$. Find the number of positive integers less than $T+36$ which have a digit sum of $14$.

solutions.title: Count
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T=60$ was passed on from A1.) We need positive integers below $96$ with digit sum $14$. One-digit numbers cannot reach $14$. For two-digit numbers $10a+b$ with $a+b=14$, $a\le9$: $59,68,77,86,95$, all below $96$. That is $5$ numbers.

**Answer: $5$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (National Final)
source.paper: 2015-16 National Final, Shuttle Round, question A3

prompt: Let $T=5$. A circle has an area of $T\pi$. Find the area of the largest square which can be drawn inside the circle.

solutions.title: Diagonal is the diameter
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T=5$ came from A2.) $\pi r^2=5\pi$ so $r^2=5$. The largest square has its diagonal equal to the diameter $2r$, so its area is $\frac12(2r)^2=2r^2=10$.

**Answer: $10$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (National Final)
source.paper: 2015-16 National Final, Shuttle Round, question A4

prompt: Let $T=10$. Four identical circles are touching inside a rectangle, as shown in the figure (the two upper circles touch each other and the top side, the two lower circles touch each other and the bottom side, each upper circle touches both lower circles, and the leftmost and rightmost circles touch the left and right sides). The radius of each circle is $\dfrac T{10}$. Write down the perimeter of the rectangle in the form $a+b\sqrt c$ where $a$ and $b$ are integers and $c$ is a prime number.

solutions.title: Centres form a rhombus
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T=10$ came from A3, so the radius is $1$.) The four centres form a rhombus of side $2$ made of two equilateral triangles. Taking the lower-left centre as origin, the centres are at horizontal positions $0,\ 1,\ 2,\ 3$ (lower-left, upper-left, lower-right, upper-right), so the rectangle's width is $3+1+1=5$. The height is the vertical separation of the rows of centres, $\sqrt3$, plus $2$ radii: $2+\sqrt3$.

Perimeter $=2(5+2+\sqrt3)=14+2\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $14+2\sqrt3$**

prompt: The expression $\dfrac{5!}{6}\times\dfrac{5}{4!}\div\dfrac{4}{3!}-\dfrac{3}{2!}+\dfrac{1!}{2}$ can be simplified to the fraction $\dfrac ab$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive integers with no common factors. Find the value of $a+b$. (Here $n!=n\times(n-1)\times\cdots\times2\times1$.)

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (National Final)
source.paper: 2015-16 National Final, Shuttle Round, question B2

prompt: Let $T=25$. Simplify $\sqrt8+\sqrt{108}\div\sqrt6+\sqrt6\times\sqrt{3T}$ into the form $a\sqrt b$, where $a$ is an integer and $b$ is a prime number. Find the value of $a$.

solutions.title: Simplify each term
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T=25$ came from B1.) $\sqrt8=2\sqrt2$; $\sqrt{108}\div\sqrt6=\sqrt{18}=3\sqrt2$; $\sqrt6\times\sqrt{75}=\sqrt{450}=15\sqrt2$. The sum is $20\sqrt2$, so $a=20$.

**Answer: $20$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (National Final)
source.paper: 2015-16 National Final, Shuttle Round, question B3

prompt: Let $T=20$. An irregular octagon has three of its exterior angles each equal to $2T^\circ$ and another four each equal to $(3T-5)^\circ$. The largest interior angle of the octagon is $A^\circ$. Find the value of $A$.

solutions.title: Exterior angles sum to 360
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T=20$ came from B2.) The three equal exterior angles are $40^\circ$, the four others $55^\circ$. These seven sum to $120+220=340$, so the eighth exterior angle is $360-340=20^\circ$. The largest interior angle goes with the smallest exterior angle: $180-20=160$.

**Answer: $160$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (National Final)
source.paper: 2015-16 National Final, Shuttle Round, question B4

prompt: Let $T=160$. The volume of a large vase is $500\text{ cm}^3$ and its surface area is $(T+40)\text{ cm}^2$. The volume of a similar vase is $108\text{ cm}^3$ and its surface area is $A\text{ cm}^2$. Find the value of $A$.

solutions.title: Scale factors
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T=160$ came from B3.) The large vase has surface area $200$. Volumes are in ratio $108:500=27:125$, so lengths are in ratio $3:5$ and areas in ratio $9:25$. Hence $A=200\times\frac9{25}=72$.

**Answer: $72$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (National Final)
source.paper: 2015-16 National Final, Shuttle Round, question C1

prompt: In the pentagon $ABCDE$, $AB$ is parallel to $DC$, $\angle DEA=\angle ABC$ and $\angle CDE$ is $40^\circ$ larger than $\angle EAB$. Also, $\angle EAB$ is twice as large as $\angle DEA$. Find the size, in degrees, of $\angle BCD$.

solutions.title: Angle sum and parallels
solutions.body:
Let $\angle DEA=e$. Then $\angle ABC=e$, $\angle EAB=2e$ and $\angle CDE=2e+40$. Since $AB\parallel DC$, the co-interior angles at $B$ and $C$ give $\angle BCD=180-e$. The angles of the pentagon sum to $540$: $e+e+2e+(2e+40)+(180-e)=540$, so $5e+220=540$, $e=64$ and $\angle BCD=116$.

**Answer: $116^\circ$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (National Final)
source.paper: 2015-16 National Final, Shuttle Round, question C2

prompt: Let $T=116$. $A$ is the number of positive integers strictly less than $\dfrac T2$ that are cubes. $B$ is the number of positive integers strictly less than $\dfrac{T+1}3$ that are triangular numbers. $C$ is the number of positive integers strictly less than $\dfrac T4$ that are primes. Find the value of $A+B+C$.

solutions.title: Count each
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T=116$ came from C1.) $A$: cubes below $58$: $1,8,27$, so $A=3$. $B$: triangular numbers below $39$: $1,3,6,10,15,21,28,36$, so $B=8$. $C$: primes below $29$: $2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23$, so $C=9$. Total $20$.

**Answer: $20$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (National Final)
source.paper: 2015-16 National Final, Shuttle Round, question C4

prompt: Let $T=10$. The diagram shows the lines $y=2x+2$ and $x+y=2T$. Write down the area of the shaded region, which is bounded by the two axes and these two lines (the region below both lines in the first quadrant).

solutions.title: Shoelace or subtraction
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T=10$ came from C3.) The lines meet where $2x+2=20-x$: $(6,14)$. The shaded region has vertices $(0,0)$, $(20,0)$, $(6,14)$, $(0,2)$.

Area $=$ triangle with vertices $(0,0),(20,0),(6,14)$ $\;(=\frac12\cdot20\cdot14=140)$ plus triangle $(0,0),(6,14),(0,2)$ $\;(=\frac12\cdot2\cdot6=6)$ $=146$.

**Answer: $146$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (National Final)
source.paper: 2015-16 National Final, Shuttle Round, question D1

prompt: The point $(1,2)$ is reflected in the line $y=5-x$ and its image is the point $(a,b)$. The point $(a,b)$ is then rotated $90^\circ$ anticlockwise about the point $(2,2)$ and its image is the point $(c,d)$. Find the value of $a+b+c+d$.

solutions.title: Do the transformations
solutions.body:
Reflection in $x+y=5$ sends $(x,y)\to(5-y,5-x)$, so $(1,2)\to(3,4)$: $a=3$, $b=4$. Relative to $(2,2)$ the point is $(1,2)$; an anticlockwise quarter turn sends $(u,v)\to(-v,u)$, giving $(-2,1)$, i.e. $(c,d)=(0,3)$. The sum is $3+4+0+3=10$.

**Answer: $10$**

solutions.title: Factor pairs of 100
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T=10$ came from D1.) $pq=T^2=100$ with $p
e q$ integers. Pairs: $(1,100),(2,50),(4,25),(5,20)$ with differences $99,48,21,15$ (negative pairs give the same differences, and $10\cdot10$ is excluded since the roots are distinct). The least difference is $15$.

**Answer: $15$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (National Final)
source.paper: 2015-16 National Final, Shuttle Round, question D3

prompt: Let $T=15$. $O$ is the centre of the circle and $B$, $D$ and $E$ lie on the circle. Lines $BC$ and $DC$ are tangents to the circle and $OE$ is parallel to $BC$. $\angle BCD=(2T+10)^\circ$. Find the size, in degrees, of $\angle CDE$.

solutions.title: Angles at the centre
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T=15$ came from D2, so $\angle BCD=40^\circ$.) The radii $OB$ and $OD$ are perpendicular to the tangents, so in quadrilateral $OBCD$: $\angle BOD=360-90-90-40=140^\circ$. Since $OE\parallel BC$ and $OB\perp BC$, $\angle BOE=90^\circ$, so $\angle EOD=140-90=50^\circ$. Triangle $OED$ is isosceles ($OE=OD$): $\angle ODE=\frac{180-50}2=65^\circ$. Since $OD\perp DC$, $\angle CDE=90-65=25^\circ$.

**Answer: $25^\circ$**

source.contest: UKMT Senior Team Maths Challenge (National Final)
source.paper: 2015-16 National Final, Shuttle Round, question D4

prompt: Let $T=25$. $ABCD$ is a trapezium in which $AB$ is parallel to $DC$. The sides $AD$ and $DC$ are both of length $(T-1)$ cm. $\angle DAB=30^\circ$ and $\angle ABC=45^\circ$. Write down the area of the trapezium, in cm$^2$, in the form $a+b\sqrt c$ where $a$ and $b$ are integers and $c$ is a prime number.

solutions.title: Height and bases
solutions.body:
(In the contest $T=25$ came from D3, so $AD=DC=24$.) The height is $24\sin30^\circ=12$. Drop perpendiculars from $D$ and $C$ to $AB$: the left overhang is $24\cos30^\circ=12\sqrt3$ and the right overhang is $12/\tan45^\circ=12$. So $AB=12\sqrt3+24+12=36+12\sqrt3$. Area $=\frac12(24+36+12\sqrt3)\cdot12=6(60+12\sqrt3)=360+72\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $360+72\sqrt3$ cm$^2$**
